Pixel Blade · the garden, restaged

Calm, but strange.

The garden survives. It just stopped being a place you could walk to.

What does a zen garden look like when dreamed of by an abstract digital artist?

Spencer Lee

The category change

Built, not found.

Every one of your five references is a stage, a gallery, or an exhibition. Nature is plinthed, backlit, printed onto screens. None of them pretends to be a location. That is not a decoration change — it moves the garden into a different category, and it settles the layer model.

Round one

Garden = grown. Photographic Kyoto at night. A real place, faithfully recorded, with one warm practical lighting it.

Now

Garden = staged. A constructed model of a place, exhibited in a void. Light is not falling on the scene — light is the scenery.

Why this is better than it sounds

Pixel Blade does not show you the buyer's world. It builds a model of that world and walks you through it — which is a fairly exact description of what advertising is. A staged garden is more honest about the business than a photographed one.

Four plates

The brief, in our palette.

Restrained pass — bronze and petrol only. The saturated version is further down, and it is the one that carries the range.

Mechanics

What makes it strange rather than pretty.

  • Constructed

    Free-standing objects in a void. No ceilings, no horizon, no building. If it reads as a location instead of an installation, it is wrong.

  • Flat planes

    Landscape as stacked cut shapes, each layer paler and hazier. No photographic terrain texture. Same plane-stacking as surreal.

  • Light is furniture

    Glowing columns, backlit discs, luminous screens. The sharpest break from night scene, where one warm practical lights a real room.

  • Mirror floor

    Seamless, black, perfectly still. Doubles the composition and the light, and removes any cue about where the viewer is standing.

  • The plinth

    Nature as an exhibited object, floating clear of the floor, lit by a single shaft.

  • Tiny figures

    scale applies unchanged — 1–4% of frame height, turned away, one to three of them.

  • Nothing happens

    No weather event, no action, no crescendo. The strangeness lives in the arrangement, never in the incident.

The color finding — this is the load-bearing one

The warm/cool split running through all five references is exactly bronze against petrol. Warm glowing objects, cool receding world.

That is the real answer to whether the garden survives the material rebuild. It survives because the staged garden and the forge run on the same two colors. A photographic garden did not — that was the range problem I flagged, and staging it is what closed it.

Still cut, and for reasons unrelated to color:

The lit world · correction

Two gamuts, one hard edge.

I had cut the coral and red outright. That was too blunt, and Spencer replaced it with a better distinction: the question is not whether those colors appear, but which side of the frame they appear on.

We're in the dark, comfy room, reading a fantastical tale of surreal dreamy exploration.

Spencer Lee

Interface gamut · the dark room

Narrow, disciplined, every pair contrast-verified. Type, tiles, buttons, rules, borders, text sections.

Image gamut · the lit world

All of the above, plus these. Permitted only inside a frame — as excitement and depth in imagery.

Two things sampling told us

This is not a foreign palette. The warm range lands at hue 12–20 — directly adjacent to bronze at hue 29. Same hue family: the interface holds it restrained, the world runs it hot. That is why a fully saturated plate still reads as this brand.

There is no pink. Nothing above hue 340 survived sampling — no true pink, no magenta. What reads as pink is a desaturated coral, #F3AF96. Worth knowing before someone reaches for an actual pink and breaks the family.

  • Falloff, not a line

    Images feather and vignette out; their own darkness is the boundary. The image emerges from the dark rather than being cut into it. A hard rectangle reads as a pasted-in photograph.

  • The feather must land

    An image's edge value has to resolve to #0A0A0B exactly. Where a plate crops lit content at its border, the vignette is mandatory — not a style choice.

  • No spill

    No saturated hue in a border, rule, tile, chip, button or label; no colored ambient light on an interface surface; no type on any part of an image still carrying chroma.

  • Bronze crosses

    It is the only color living in both gamuts — restrained in the room, hot in the world. That is what stitches them together, and nothing else gets the privilege.

  • Rationing is the point

    The interface is monastic so the images can be lush. Spend the saturated range in the room and it stops being an event — the accent-word rule at the scale of a whole page.

  • Page rhythm

    Long quiet dark passages punctuated by contained saturated apertures. The images are the exhalations — a rhythm nobody had to invent.

The ceiling · measured

The limit is coverage, not chroma.

You said there is no upper ceiling on imagery, and that if one were needed it would be your very first reference. Measuring the whole ladder showed why both halves of that are right — and that I had been watching the wrong axis.

Measured across the plates · brand/check-plate.py
PlateChroma coverageDark groundPeak sat
Columns — restrained21.7%62.8%70
Columns — warm33.6%53.8%79
Enso — hot36.1%45.6%92
Ceiling21.4%50.9%89
Aperture19.5%62.4%95

The ceiling plate has the lowest coverage in the set

It runs near the top on saturation and near the bottom on area. It reads as maximal because it is jewelled — intense chroma in small discrete objects separated by void — not because it is bright.

So the bounds are on area: saturated coverage ≤ 25%, dark ground ≥ 50%, peak saturation unbounded. By that measure my Enso and warm Columns plates are already past the limit and the ceiling plate is comfortably inside it — the exact opposite of how they look.

And you were right about the edge.

We feather in, and vignette in the edges so it's not a hard line of light against our moonlit candle night.

Spencer Lee

I had written "hard edge, never a gradient." That was wrong, and the measurement caught it independently: the ceiling plate crops lit lanterns at its border, so its corners average #4B3525 — a delta of 65 from the page ground. Butted against the room it would have shown a visible seam.

Both rules are enforced by brand/check-plate.py, and brand/feather.py applies the falloff. The checker fails on coverage and on the edge seam, and never on saturation.

One fork

Photograph, or illustration?

Both satisfy the brief. They are different worlds, and the site can only be one of them.

A · Photographs of impossible things

Enso, Columns, Specimen. Rendered as though a camera were present in a place that cannot exist. Weight, atmosphere, real optics.

Harder to produce consistently. Ages better. Sits naturally under the dark elegance treatment.

B · Flat graphic worlds

Planes. Landscape as printed shapes, no camera implied. Closest to the literal reading of "dreamed by an abstract digital artist."

Cheaper to extend, easier to keep consistent, and can be built in code rather than generated — which matters for a parallax environment.

    How strong a feather?

    The default inset takes the ceiling plate from 21% chroma coverage to 7.6% — a lot of the image given back to the dark. A lighter setting lands at 11.9% and still passes. Worth picking a house default.
